concepts.def: One star, the Sun, together with the eight planets and the dwarf planets that orbit around the Sun, plus the natural satellites (moons) that orbit those planets.
A large body in orbit around the Sun. There are eight planets in our solar system.
A smaller body that orbits the Sun and is counted as part of the solar system but is not one of the eight planets.
A moon: a body that orbits a planet rather than orbiting the Sun directly. Natural satellites are part of the solar system.
A body, such as the Sun, in which fusion reactions release energy. Our solar system contains exactly one star.
The galaxy that contains our solar system. Our solar system is only a small part of it.
A cloud of dust and gas in space. The Sun was formed from a nebula pulled together by gravitational attraction.
The attractive force between masses. It is the force that pulls the dust and gas of a nebula together to begin a star.
The hot, dense body formed as gravity pulls a cloud of dust and gas together, before fusion reactions begin.
A reaction in which small nuclei join to form a larger nucleus, releasing energy. Fusion begins once gravity has made a protostar hot and dense enough.
The balance in a stable star between the gravitational collapse pulling it inwards and the expansion caused by the energy released by fusion.
The long, stable stage of a star's life during which the inward gravitational collapse and the outward expansion due to fusion energy are in equilibrium.
The sequence of stages a star passes through. Which sequence a star follows is determined by the size of the star.
The stage a star about the size of the Sun swells into when it leaves the main sequence.
The small, dense remnant left when a red giant of about the Sun's size collapses at the end of its life.
The cold, non-luminous remnant a white dwarf becomes once it has cooled down completely.
The stage a star much more massive than the Sun swells into when it leaves the main sequence.
The explosion of a massive star. It produces the elements heavier than iron and distributes all the elements throughout the universe.
The extremely dense remnant left at the centre after a supernova.
The remnant left after the supernova of the most massive stars, whose gravity is so strong that light cannot escape.
Fusion processes in stars produce all of the naturally occurring elements; elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova.
A man-made object placed in orbit around a planet, held in that orbit by gravity in the same way as a moon.
A path around a larger body in which the distance from that body stays the same, maintained by the force of gravity.
Speed is how fast something moves; velocity is speed in a stated direction. A change of direction alone changes the velocity.
An orbit that repeats indefinitely. For a stable orbit the radius must change if the orbital speed changes.

mcqs.q: Which list correctly describes what our solar system contains?
options: One star, the eight planets, the dwarf planets and the planets' moons
One star and the eight planets that orbit around it, nothing else
One star, nine planets including Pluto, and the moons of those
Eight planets and their moons, with the Sun counted as a planet
mcqs.explain: This is exactly the membership the specification gives: one star, the Sun, the eight planets, the dwarf planets, and the natural satellites that orbit planets.

mcqs.q: What is meant by a natural satellite?
options: A small rocky body that orbits the Sun directly, between the planets
A dwarf planet, which orbits the Sun beyond the eight planets
A moon: a body that orbits a planet rather than orbiting the Sun
A man-made craft kept in orbit by its engines, not gravity
mcqs.explain: The specification defines natural satellites as the moons that orbit planets, and states that they are part of the solar system.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes how our solar system relates to the Milky Way?
options: The Milky Way is just another name for our own solar system
Our solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy
The Milky Way galaxy holds everything in the universe
Our solar system lies at the exact centre of the Milky Way
mcqs.explain: The specification states directly that our solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy.

mcqs.q: How was the Sun formed?
options: From a cloud of dust and gas squeezed together by magnetism
From a huge ball of chemical fuel that was set alight in space
From a cloud of dust and gas in which fusion started at once
From a cloud of dust and gas pulled together by gravity
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the Sun was formed from a cloud of dust and gas (nebula) pulled together by gravitational attraction.

mcqs.q: At the start of a star's life cycle, why do fusion reactions begin?
options: Gravity draws the dust and gas together, heating it until nuclei fuse
The dust and gas catch fire and burn chemically, giving out the energy
Fusion starts as soon as gravity begins to draw the cloud inwards
Magnetic forces squeeze the cloud until its particles join together
mcqs.explain: Gravitational attraction pulls the material of the nebula together; the compression raises the temperature and density until fusion reactions start.

mcqs.q: Which two effects are in equilibrium in a stable star?
options: No effects at all, because equilibrium means no forces act on it
The inward pull of gravity and the outward push of gravity itself
The weight of the star and the upthrust of the gas around it
The gravitational collapse inwards and the expansion due to fusion energy
mcqs.explain: The specification states that fusion reactions lead to an equilibrium between the gravitational collapse of a star and its expansion due to fusion energy.

mcqs.q: A main sequence star stays the same size for billions of years. Why?
options: No forces act inside a star once it reaches the main sequence
Its inward collapse and its outward expansion stay balanced
Gravity pushes the star outwards as hard as it pulls it inwards
The upthrust of the gas around it supports the star's weight
mcqs.explain: While fusion continues at a steady rate, the expansion due to fusion energy exactly balances the gravitational collapse, so the star's size does not change.

mcqs.q: What determines the life cycle that a star will follow?
options: The colour of the star, which shows its surface state
How bright the star looks when viewed from Earth
The size of the star, which sets the path it takes
The age of the star, since all stars follow one path
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the life cycle of a star is determined by the size of the star.

mcqs.q: A star about the size of the Sun leaves the main sequence. What happens next?
options: It explodes straight away as a supernova
It shrinks back to become a protostar
It becomes a white dwarf at once
It expands and becomes a red giant
mcqs.explain: For a star of about the Sun's size, the stage after the main sequence is the red giant.

mcqs.q: What is the full sequence of stages at the end of the life of a star about the size of the Sun?
options: Red giant, then white dwarf, then black dwarf
Red giant, then supernova, then a neutron star
Red super giant, then supernova, then black hole
White dwarf, then red giant, then a black dwarf
mcqs.explain: A star of about the Sun's size swells into a red giant, collapses to a white dwarf, and finally cools to a black dwarf.

mcqs.q: What happens to a star much more massive than the Sun after the main sequence?
options: Red giant, then white dwarf, then black dwarf, just as the Sun will
Red super giant, then supernova, then neutron star or black hole
Red super giant, then supernova, then always a black hole
Red super giant, then protostar, then a new main sequence star
mcqs.explain: A star much more massive than the Sun becomes a red super giant, explodes as a supernova, and leaves a neutron star or a black hole.

mcqs.q: What can be left at the centre after a massive star explodes as a supernova?
options: A black hole, whatever the mass of the star that exploded
A white dwarf that later cools to become a black dwarf
A neutron star, or a black hole if the star was massive enough
Nothing at all, as the star is completely destroyed
mcqs.explain: A supernova leaves a very dense neutron star, and for the most massive stars a black hole.

mcqs.q: Which elements are produced by fusion processes in stars?
options: Only hydrogen and helium, and nothing more
Only those elements that are heavier than iron
All of the naturally occurring elements
Only elements made by the splitting of nuclei
mcqs.explain: The specification states that fusion processes in stars produce all of the naturally occurring elements.

mcqs.q: Where are the elements heavier than iron produced?
options: In the explosion of a massive star, a supernova
In the fusion reactions inside a main sequence star
Nowhere; they have existed from the very start
By the splitting of very large nuclei inside the star
mcqs.explain: The specification states that elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova.

mcqs.q: What does the explosion of a massive star do to the elements it has produced?
options: It leaves the elements locked inside the remnant star
It distributes the elements throughout the whole universe
It destroys the elements, leaving only hydrogen gas
It converts all the elements into ones lighter than iron
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the explosion of a massive star (supernova) distributes the elements throughout the universe.

mcqs.q: How do fusion processes in stars lead to the formation of new elements?
options: Large nuclei split apart to form smaller nuclei of new elements
Atoms join chemically to make new compounds and elements
Fusion makes only the elements heavier than iron in the core
Small nuclei join to form larger nuclei of different elements
mcqs.explain: In fusion, small nuclei join to form a larger nucleus. Because the number of protons changes, the new nucleus is a nucleus of a different element.

mcqs.q: What allows a planet or a satellite to maintain a circular orbit?
options: Gravity provides the force that keeps it in its circular orbit
There is no gravity in space, so it just keeps drifting round
Its engines fire all the time to hold it in its orbital path
An outward force balances gravity and holds it in place
mcqs.explain: The specification states that gravity provides the force that allows planets and satellites, both natural and artificial, to maintain their circular orbits.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly compares moons and artificial satellites?
options: Both orbit a planet, but only the moon is held there by gravity
Both orbit a planet; moons are natural and satellites are man-made
Both orbit the Sun directly, and both were formed with the Sun
Neither one is held by gravity, since gravity does not act in space
mcqs.explain: Moons and artificial satellites both orbit a planet and are both held in orbit by gravity. The distinction is that moons are natural and satellites are made by people.

mcqs.q: (HT only) A satellite travels round a circular orbit at a steady rate. Which statement is correct?
options: Its speed and its velocity are both remaining constant
Its speed keeps increasing because gravity acts upon it
Its speed stays the same but its velocity is changing
Its velocity is constant but its speed is changing
mcqs.explain: In a circular orbit gravity acts at right angles to the motion, so it changes the direction of travel and therefore the velocity, while the speed is unchanged.

mcqs.q: (HT only) A satellite in a stable circular orbit is made to travel faster. For the orbit to stay stable, what must happen?
options: The radius of the orbit must become much larger
The radius of the orbit can stay exactly as before
The orbit turns into a straight line at once
The radius of the orbit must get smaller
mcqs.explain: For a stable orbit the radius must change if the speed changes: a faster orbital speed corresponds to a smaller orbital radius.
